page.mentor_intro: Retrieved evidence centres on outcomes rather than the diagnostic pathway: type A dissection carries organ-specific malperfusion risk that predicts in-hospital death, and for type B the question is whether and when to add TEVAR to medical therapy. Guideline-level recommendations were not in the retrieved set.

teaching_points.claim: In acute type A aortic dissection, in-hospital survival varies with the type of malperfusion; mesenteric, coronary and cerebral malperfusion carried the highest in-hospital mortality, so organ-specific malperfusion should inform perioperative risk and surgical planning.
Women with type A dissection more often had pericardial effusion or tamponade, while in-hospital surgical mortality did not differ by sex (RR 1.02), suggesting a personalised approach.

A meta-analysis found TEVAR was associated with lower mortality than best medical therapy in type B dissection, especially in patients aged 65 or older, at the cost of longer hospital and ICU stays, with randomised trials still needed.

For uncomplicated type B dissection, the role of TEVAR remains debated: it improves aortic remodelling but there is no definitive survival evidence, and trials and guidelines that include high-risk features are needed.
Meta-analyses of TEVAR timing found the subacute phase (14-90 days from onset) associated with better long-term outcomes, including lower aortic-related death and reintervention.
Retrograde type A dissection after TEVAR is rare but carries high mortality (about 42%), especially in the first month and with proximal bare-stent grafts.
The GERAADA score showed better calibration than EuroSCORE II for 30-day mortality after surgery for acute type A dissection, though discrimination of both was moderate.
AI tools can feasibly detect aortic dissection on CT but do not yet demonstrate clinical applicability, and most studies were low quality.

uncertainties: Whether pre-emptive TEVAR improves survival in uncomplicated type B dissection.
mcq_angles: Malperfusion type and operative mortality in type A dissection.
Timing of TEVAR in type B dissection.
case_hooks: Type A dissection with mesenteric malperfusion on CT angiography.
page.gaps: Presentation, the diagnostic pathway (CT angiography, D-dimer), blood-pressure and heart-rate targets with beta-blockers, indications for emergency surgery and classification systems are not stated in the retrieved abstract excerpts. Needs the ESC 2024 or ACC/AHA 2022 aortic guideline before approval.

page.mentor_intro: Acute asthma care centres on bronchodilators and systemic corticosteroids; high-dose inhaled corticosteroids may add benefit, and IV magnesium helps children. Prevention depends on adherence, eosinophilic phenotype and inhaler technique.

teaching_points.claim: A meta-analysis found moderate evidence that high-dose inhaled corticosteroids added to systemic corticosteroids reduce hospital admission (OR 0.73) in ED treatment of moderate-to-severe exacerbations.
In children, intravenous magnesium sulfate improved pulmonary function and reduced hospitalisation and further treatment, whereas nebulised magnesium had no significant effect.

The Italian paediatric acute-asthma guideline advises against epinephrine, allows IV magnesium sulfate in severe attacks or FEV1 below 60% unresponsive to inhaled therapy, allows heliox in life-threatening attacks, and does not recommend leukotriene receptor antagonists.
Adherence of 80% or more lowered the odds of severe exacerbation (OR 0.53), and discontinuing therapy raised it.
Blood eosinophils of 200 cells/microlitre or more are associated with exacerbation (a modifiable factor in asthma management).
Inhaler technique education reduced exacerbation rates in older adults with asthma or COPD (pooled risk ratio 0.71).
Oral timolol and infusion propranolol were associated with higher asthma attack risk and should be avoided in patients at risk of asthma.
GORD and asthma exacerbation are only weakly associated.

uncertainties: Optimal role of inhaled steroids in the emergency department.
case_hooks: Child with severe attack unresponsive to initial inhaled therapy.
page.gaps: Severity classification, oxygen targets, nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium dosing, oral steroid doses, and escalation to ventilation are not stated in the retrieved abstract excerpts. Needs the BTS/SIGN or GINA acute asthma sections.

topic: best initial test for suspected pulmonary embolism in a stable patient

page.mentor_intro: In a haemodynamically stable patient the first step is a pre-test probability assessment, then D-dimer in non-high probability, then imaging. Age-adjusted D-dimer and the YEARS algorithm reduce imaging while staying safe.

teaching_points.claim: Original and simplified Wells rules combined with age-adjusted D-dimer have similar performance for ruling out PE, and the simplified Wells rule is preferred for ease of use.
Age-adjusted D-dimer cutoffs combined with low clinical probability rule out PE with fewer false positives than conventional D-dimer, across 47,720 patients with non-high clinical probability.
The YEARS algorithm had pooled sensitivity of 96% and specificity of 50%, with a risk ratio of 0.78 for advanced imaging use, suggesting it is effective and safe.
D-dimer interpretation depends on assay performance characteristics, and international guidelines differ in how they allow age-adjusted and pretest-adjusted thresholds.
In pregnancy, introducing the pregnancy-adapted YEARS guideline increased investigation for PE, and over 5 years there were no known missed cases among women assessed with D-dimer alone.

In cancer patients, D-dimer with clinical decision rules had failure rates similar to standard imaging, with the highest yield (26%) from revised Geneva with age-adjusted D-dimer and the YEARS algorithm.
In COVID-19, D-dimer of at least 1000 micrograms/L may help select patients for CT pulmonary angiography.
Double low-dose CT pulmonary angiography is feasible, with reduced radiation and contrast dose without compromising diagnostic image quality.

uncertainties: Optimal D-dimer thresholds in special populations.
case_hooks: Stable patient with pleuritic pain and low Wells score.
page.gaps: PERC, the age-adjusted formula (age x 10 micrograms/L above 50), Wells and Geneva score components, V/Q scanning and CTPA pathways are not stated in the retrieved abstract excerpts.

topic: Cushings disease: pituitary source, inferior petrosal sinus sampling, transsphenoidal surgery

page.mentor_intro: Distinguishing pituitary from ectopic ACTH source relies on dynamic testing, pituitary MRI and bilateral inferior petrosal sinus sampling (BIPSS). BIPSS has high diagnostic accuracy for confirming a pituitary source but its tumour lateralisation may not predict surgical remission.

teaching_points.claim: A meta-analysis of BIPSS in ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome found sensitivity 0.94 and specificity 0.89, and concluded it should be used to identify the ACTH source.
IPSS tumour lateralisation was not clearly associated with postoperative remission or cure, questioning its use for surgical planning rather than confirming a pituitary source.
Prolactin adjustment in BIPSS improved sensitivity for Cushing disease (difference 5.39%) but did not help identify ectopic ACTH syndrome.
Desmopressin-stimulated IPSS shows improved diagnostic performance relative to CRH stimulation, with pooled positive predictive value trends.
In dynamic testing, a positive ACTH response after the CRH test makes Cushing disease highly likely; high-dose dexamethasone suppression and desmopressin tests were less accurate than CRH testing.
Detection of an adenoma on MRI improves the chance of curative resection in Cushing disease.
The 10 microgram desmopressin test has low confidence in its estimated accuracy, as prediction intervals were wide.
The 2008 Endocrine Society screening recommendations for Cushing syndrome are still considered valid in 2022.
Etomidate effectively and safely reduces cortisol in severe Cushing syndrome, and mifepristone needs close monitoring for cortisol withdrawal, hypokalaemia and antiprogesterone effects.

uncertainties: Value of IPSS lateralisation for surgery.
mcq_angles: BIPSS to separate pituitary from ectopic ACTH.
case_hooks: ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome with negative pituitary MRI.
page.gaps: Transsphenoidal surgery remission rates, post-operative cortisol thresholds, adrenal insufficiency management and second-line options are not stated in the retrieved abstract excerpts.

topic: should I start an SGLT2 inhibitor for my patient with HFrEF?

page.mentor_intro: SGLT2 inhibitors reduce heart failure events and improve functional capacity, quality of life and cardiac remodelling in HFrEF. Early in-hospital initiation was associated with fewer readmissions in meta-analysis, and safety has been acceptable with MRA co-treatment.

teaching_points.claim: A large meta-analysis found SGLT2 inhibitors reduced heart failure events and cardiovascular death in people with heart failure, with consistent effects across a wide range of subgroups.
SGLT2 inhibitors improved exercise capacity (6-minute walk distance) and KCCQ quality-of-life scores, regardless of sex or ejection fraction.
In HFrEF, SGLT2 inhibitors improved cardiac structure and function, with a rise in LVEF (about 2.7%) and a fall in left atrial volume index.

In patients recently hospitalised for acute heart failure, early SGLT2 inhibitor initiation was associated with fewer heart failure readmissions (RR 0.79) and acute kidney injury, with decongestive effects.
The DAPA ACT HF-TIMI 68 trial found in-hospital dapagliflozin did not significantly reduce cardiovascular death or worsening heart failure at 2 months, though pooled trial data suggest early benefit.
MRAs did not alter SGLT2 inhibitor effects, and SGLT2 inhibitors attenuated MRA-associated hyperkalaemia.
In older or frail patients with type 2 diabetes and heart failure, SGLT2 inhibitors were linked to lower total mortality without a significant increase in ketoacidosis or acute kidney injury.

uncertainties: Magnitude of benefit with in-hospital initiation.
mcq_angles: SGLT2 inhibitors as part of HFrEF quadruple therapy.
case_hooks: Recently hospitalised HFrEF patient on ACE inhibitor, beta-blocker and MRA.
page.gaps: Eligibility thresholds (eGFR), starting doses, sick-day rules, genital infection and ketoacidosis counselling and the pivotal DAPA-HF and EMPEROR-Reduced results are not stated in the retrieved abstract excerpts.

topic: Obesity pharmacotherapy: orlistat, GLP-1 agonists, naltrexone-bupropion indications and outcomes

page.mentor_intro: Pharmacotherapy is now an integral part of obesity treatment: GLP-1 receptor agonists and tirzepatide produce the largest weight loss, phentermine-topiramate is also effective, and gastrointestinal effects are the main adverse effects.

teaching_points.claim: The 2025 Canadian guideline update says clinicians should use pharmacotherapy as an integral part of obesity treatment and recommends against compounded medications or medications not approved for weight loss.
A network meta-analysis found phentermine-topiramate and GLP-1 receptor agonists the best at reducing weight, with semaglutide possibly the most effective of the GLP-1 agonists.

Tirzepatide 15 mg had the highest efficacy for achieving at least 15% weight loss (risk ratio 10.24 versus placebo), with significantly more gastrointestinal adverse effects for tirzepatide and GLP-1 agonists.
GLP-1 receptor agonists significantly reduced weight, BMI and waist circumference, with greatest benefit in younger, female, non-diabetic patients and longer treatment.
In non-diabetic patients with overweight or obesity, GLP-1 agonists produced several gastrointestinal adverse effects, and risk profiles differ by agent.

Semaglutide reduced heart failure hospitalisation (76%), cardiovascular death (17%), all-cause death (21%), non-fatal MI (24%) and stroke (35% in diabetes) in a pooled analysis, with higher adverse-effect frequency.
RCTs show no likely increase in suicide-related adverse events with GLP-1 agonists, though monitoring continues.
In children and adolescents, GLP-1 agonists improved glycaemic, weight and cardiometabolic outcomes in a meta-analysis of 18 trials.

uncertainties: Long-term durability and weight regain after stopping.
mcq_angles: Choosing a GLP-1 agonist or tirzepatide.
case_hooks: Adult with BMI 36 and prediabetes after failed lifestyle intervention.
page.gaps: Orlistat and naltrexone-bupropion are not covered by the retrieved excerpts, nor are indications and BMI thresholds, contraindications (pancreatitis, thyroid cancer history) or dosing.

topic: Community-acquired pneumonia: CURB-65, PSI, empirical therapy, atypical pathogens
cluster: Community-acquired pneumonia: CURB-65, PSI, empirical therapy, atypical pathogens

guidelinesKept: Diagnosis and Treatment of Adults with Community-acquired Pneumonia: An Official Clinical Practice Guideline of the American Thoracic Society and Infectious Diseases Society of America.
BTS guidelines for the management of community acquired pneumonia in adults: update 2009.

page.mentor_intro: Objective risk assessment in community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) guides site-of-care decisions, reducing avoidable hospital admissions and associated nosocomial complications. The two primary validated scoring systems are CURB-65 and the Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI). CURB-65 assigns 1 point each for Confusion, Urea >7 mmol/L (BUN >19 mg/dL), Respiratory rate >=30/min, Blood pressure (SBP <90 or DBP <=60 mmHg), and Age >=65; scores 0-1 indicate outpatient management, score 2 warrants short inpatient or supervised care, and scores 3-5 mandate inpatient treatment with consideration of ICU admission. PSI incorporates 20 variables and demonstrates higher sensitivity for safely triaging low-risk patients (Classes I-III) to outpatient care. Empiric therapy must cover atypical pathogens (Mycoplasma, Chlamydophila, Legionella), which lack peptidoglycan cell walls and are inherently resistant to beta-lactam antimicrobials, requiring macrolides, tetracyclines, or fluoroquinolones.

teaching_points.claim: The CURB-65 severity score stratifies 30-day mortality from 0.7% (score 0) to >30% (score 4-5), guiding triage: scores 0-1 are suitable for outpatient therapy, score 2 requires inpatient consideration, and scores >=3 indicate severe CAP.

The Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) stratifies patients into 5 mortality risk classes; the ATS/IDSA guidelines recommend PSI over CURB-65 because PSI identifies a larger proportion of low-risk patients (Classes I-II) who can be safely treated at home.

Atypical pneumonia pathogens (Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydophila pneumoniae, Legionella pneumophila) lack peptidoglycan cell walls and are inherently resistant to all beta-lactam antibiotics, mandating protein-synthesis or DNA-gyrase inhibitors.

In patients with severe CAP (CURB-65 >=3), combination therapy with a beta-lactam plus a macrolide reduces mortality compared to beta-lactam monotherapy, driven by atypical coverage and immunomodulatory anti-inflammatory effects of macrolides.
